articles.title: Horário eleitoral do 1ºturno das Eleições 2026 termina hoje; entenda | G1
articles.standfirst: Propaganda gratuita no rádio e na televisão chega à reta final antes da votação de domingo
articles.summary: Propaganda gratuita no rádio e na televisão chega à reta final antes da votação de domingo
articles.body:
Lula, Flávio, Cury e Caiado no horário eleitoral de TV — Foto: Reprodução

O horário eleitoral gratuito das Eleições 2026 no rádio e na televisão termina nesta quinta-feira (1º), três dias antes do primeiro turno, marcado para domingo (4). A data vale para a propaganda eleitoral gratuita referente ao primeiro turno.

A propaganda no rádio e na TV começou em 28 de agosto e, durante esse período, candidatos aos cargos em disputa tiveram espaço reservado para apresentar suas campanhas ao eleitorado.

O calendário do Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE) estabelece 1º de outubro como o último dia de divulgação da propaganda eleitoral gratuita no rádio e na televisão relativa ao primeiro turno.

Se a disputa para Presidente da República ou governador tiver segundo turno, a propaganda eleitoral gratuita volta a ser exibida no rádio e na televisão a partir de 9 de outubro.

Nesse caso, os candidatos que participarem da segunda etapa da eleição terão propaganda até 23 de outubro, dois dias antes da votação, marcada para 25 de outubro.

A propaganda do segundo turno, portanto, não começa automaticamente para todos os cargos. Ela ocorre somente onde houver segundo turno.

1º de outubro : último dia do horário eleitoral gratuito no rádio e na TV para o primeiro turno.

4 de outubro : primeiro turno das eleições.

9 a 23 de outubro : caso haja segundo turno, volta a propaganda eleitoral gratuita no rádio e na TV.

23 de outubro : último dia do horário eleitoral para o segundo turno.

25 de outubro : data prevista para o eventual segundo turno.

O horário eleitoral acaba junto com toda a propaganda política?

Não necessariamente. O calendário eleitoral estabelece diferentes prazos para as modalidades de propaganda.

Em 1º de outubro, além de ser o último dia do horário eleitoral gratuito no rádio e na TV, também termina o período para a realização de comícios e para a utilização de aparelhagem de sonorização fixa, observadas as regras eleitorais. A data também marca o último dia para debates no rádio e na televisão, que podem se estender até as 7h de 2 de outubro.

Já a distribuição de material gráfico pode ocorrer até 3 de outubro, véspera do primeiro turno, conforme as regras do calendário eleitoral.

articles.title: Christa Pike’s failed execution follows another in Tennessee this year
articles.summary: In May, officials called off the lethal injection of Tony Carruthers, after failing to place an IV.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — Christa Pike remained in a hospital Thursday after Tennessee’s attempt to execute her failed, marking the second unsuccessful execution attempt in the state this year.

Pike, the lone woman on Tennessee’s death row , was injected twice with lethal drugs Wednesday night but did not die. The state later transported her to an off-site medical facility for care.

Her failed execution comes months after Tennessee also called off the execution of death row inmate Tony Carruthers after medical personnel struggled to establish the required IV access.

Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee said the state’s remaining scheduled execution of 2026 will now be called off and ordered a third-party review. Pike’s attorneys said they had not been told her condition.

Pike was scheduled to become the first woman Tennessee executed in more than 200 years, according to historical records.

Tony Carruthers’ execution also called off

In May, state officials called off the lethal injection of Tony Carruthers, who was convicted of kidnapping and killing three people in 1994, after executioners tried and failed for over an hour to place an IV to administer pentobarbital.

Carruthers’ sister, Dr. Tonya Hervey, later filed a complaint with the Tennessee Department of Health alleging that the failed execution caused serious injuries to her brother, according to WSMV-TV .

Hervey said she believes Carruthers suffered a stroke that left him partially paralyzed and described him as experiencing extreme pain during the procedure. She alleged medical personnel attempted multiple methods to establish access before the execution was called off after about 90 minutes.

In a complaint, Hervey wrote Carruthers can no longer use his right hand, drags his right leg when walking, and has experienced changes in his balance, personality and cognitive functioning.

The Tennessee Department of Health said it reviews complaints and assigns priority based on the severity of the alleged violation before being sent to a regional office for investigation.

Doctor involved in Carruthers’ execution was also planned in Pike’s

Dr. Mark Walton Fowler, the Tennessee Department of Corrections physician involved in Carruthers’ failed execution attempt, was also planned to be involved in Pike’s execution, NBC News reported .

Fowler’s role in Carruthers’ failed execution has drawn scrutiny. Hervey accused Fowler of malpractice and torture in a complaint filed with the Tennessee Department of Health, alleging he struggled to establish additional access during the procedure before the execution was called off.

The Tennessee Department of Corrections has not commented on whether Fowler was involved in Pike’s execution or whether his role changed following the failed attempt to execute Carruthers.

articles.title: FCC chief: Taxpayer-funded ads touting Trump ‘don’t raise any red flags’

The ad, paid for by the U.S. government, blasts communism, socialism and Marxism in the U.S. and casts the president in a positive light…
articles.body:
Federal Communications Commission (FCC) head Brendan Carr swatted away concerns about a pro-Trump TV advertisement billed as a public service announcement that sparked outrage from Democrats and government watchdogs this week.

The ad, paid for by the U.S. government , blasts communism, socialism and Marxism in the U.S. and casts the president in a positive light with less than a month before the midterm elections.

Trump is heard on the ad saying “together we will defeat communism, socialism and Marxism in America” and, “America will never be a communist country.”

Asked about complaints from the activist group Public Citizen and others about the ads, Carr said the ad struck him as “normal course public service announcements that you see all the time.”

And Carr demurred when asked about Republicans on Capitol Hill who have expressed discomfort with the ad.

“There’s nothing in there that strikes me as out of the ordinary or that would merit any sort of FCC review,” Carr said of the ad that has aired on a number of broadcast and cable channels. “There are groups on the left that have long worked and pushed to weaponize the FCC’s license renewal process. I’m sure they’ll do it again in the future. Again with respect to these, they are normal PSAs that don’t raise any red flags.”

Carr is a Trump ally who has launched investigations into several media companies with news and entertainment divisions that publish reporting and commentary critical of the president.

He has vowed to ensure broadcasters are serving the “public interest” and called for the firing of ABC comedian Jimmy Kimmel over comments he made about the Republican response to the assassination of conservative activist Charlie Kirk.

Disney, which owns ABC, is currently suing Trump’s FCC for what it says is targeting the media conglomerate for license renewal based on the broadcasters editorial decisions.

A hearing in that case is slated for next week.

articles.title: Supreme Court takes up Trump’s mandatory detention policy
articles.summary: The Supreme Court announced Thursday it will decide the legality of President Trump’s mandatory detention policy, putting one of his banner immigration programs on the justices’ docket for their upcoming term. The Trump administration argues it can detain people without bond if they’re found to be in the country unlawfully, even if they have been living on…
articles.body:
The Supreme Court announced Thursday it will decide the legality of President Trump’s mandatory detention policy, putting one of his banner immigration programs on the justices’ docket for their upcoming term.

The Trump administration argues it can detain people without bond if they’re found to be in the country unlawfully, even if they have been living on U.S. soil for years.

It’s a significant expansion of the government’s immigration powers. The push has fueled thousands of cases claiming the policy exceeds federal law, creating an avalanche of work for judges across the country, who are racing to keep up .

The case marks another major confrontation between the Trump administration and the conservative-majority court. However, the justices opted against taking up a broader legal question of whether Trump’s policy violates constitutional due process protections. As of now, the court will only decide if the policy follows federal law.

The dispute is set to be heard during the Supreme Court’s upcoming term. Oral arguments are expected early next year, with a decision likely by summer.

Circuit courts have mostly ruled against the president . The Trump administration brought the battle to the justices after losing before the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 2nd Circuit.

Solicitor General D. John Sauer said it’s “disrupting the orderly administration of immigration law.”

“Moreover, the volume of habeas litigation will continue to impose immense burdens on district courts and U.S. Attorney’s Offices throughout the nation until this issue is resolved,” Sauer wrote in court filings.

Under previous administrations, those who were detained had a right to push for their release from detention in front of an immigration judge.

Detention rates under Trump have skyrocketed, with more than 65,000 people held in facilities across the country.

Advocates for immigrants have noted that the vast majority of those detained migrants — roughly 70 percent — have no criminal convictions. Many are also legal immigrants, including those who have active immigration petitions that have not yet been acted on because of administrative backlogs.

In the most recent ruling from the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit, the court noted the “tsunami” of habeas petitions spurred by the administration’s new interpretation.

“Hundreds of federal district courts have considered the question we consider today. The overwhelming majority — over five hundred — rejected the Government’s new construction and sided with the petitioners in over twenty thousand individual cases,” the appeals court wrote.

But they determined Congress did not give the department authority to broadly detain every migrant in passing the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act (IIRIRA).

“If we were to agree with the Government’s construction, we would need to conclude that, in passing IIRIRA thirty years ago, Congress intended to direct the single largest mass detention of human beings in our nation’s history,” they wrote.

In taking up the battle on Thursday, the Supreme Court only agreed to decide whether Trump’s policy violates the IIRIA.

Some individuals have separately advanced arguments that the policy, regardless, violates their due process rights under the Constitution.

articles.title: Healthcare could be Republicans’ final nail in the coffin this November
articles.summary: For the past 15 years, Republican health care policy has been simple: ObamaCare stinks (end of policy). But that’s not just working, and it’s adding to their troubles in the 2026 midterms.
articles.body:
For the past 15 years, Republican health care policy has been simple: ObamaCare stinks (end of policy).

But that’s not just working, and it’s adding to their troubles in the 2026 midterms.

Health insurance premiums for 2027 are rocketing, and the announcements are arriving right before the November elections. Businesses are looking at an 8 percent hike , well above inflation. And some of that cost will be passed on to employees. Premiums for individuals through the marketplace are going up, too — an average of 16 percent in Pennsylvania , 15 percent in Ohio, and between 12 and 16 percent in Iowa. Everyone is going to feel the pain.

Sure, President Trump cut some deals for cheaper drugs for Medicaid and discounts via Trump Rx coupons . But those deals have barely dented the real cost. Yes, the Bureau of Labor Statistics claims health care inflation is down. Conveniently, the Consumer Price Index includes only a portion of health insurance premiums. Inconveniently for Trump and the Republicans, people still have to pay those premiums in full — and they are going up.

This is all reminiscent of the Biden administration. Recall Team Biden stubbornly insisting inflation was not a problem — just fake news by right-wing propagandists. What the non-geniuses on Team Biden forgot was that the consumer price index doesn’t include interest rates, which more than doubled . That means out-of-pocket costs for buying and financing a house — or anything else financed — went up more than 80 percent.

But consumers don’t care about government reports or dry statistical releases. They look at their bank accounts and their monthly expenses. If they are falling behind, no amount of blustering and denial is going to convince them otherwise.

Even more ominously for Trump and the Republican Party is what happened to Biden in the fall of 2023. As I once noted , Biden’s polling against Trump took a huge hit in key swing states. I attributed that to the Hamas attacks against Israel and an intensifying immigration crisis. But the health care premium increases for 2024 were announced at that time, too. And those hikes were big .

Denial and accusations of corporate greed didn’t save Biden or Kamala Harris. They’re not going to work for Trump and the Republicans, either.

The disgrace of it all is that Republicans had their opportunities — they just don’t do anything. It is a cheap line, but nothing is “affordable” about the Affordable Care Act. Former President Barack Obama was notably disinterested in the price side of the equation. Suspiciously timed to commence after his 2012 re-election campaign, ObamaCare has done nothing in the last 14 years to arrest the rise in health care costs and insurance premiums.

Although productivity and innovation led to gains and low inflation in the economy (at least through 2020), healthcare has stood out as totally resistant to these trends everywhere else. It is just as bureaucratic, wasteful and non-competitive as ever. ObamaCare has done nothing to assuage Americans’ concerns over health care.

Voters have consistently cited health care as a top issue. In its Sept. 14 benchmark, YouGov found health care to be the third most important issue — exactly where it was six months ago. And these results mask the true level of concern.

Health care concerns are tied up with cost pressures, that is to say, inflation. YouGov has inflation as the top issue by far, two and a half times higher than “jobs and the economy,” the second most important issue. Six months ago, inflation was on top, twice as important as “jobs and the economy.” A Center Square poll has 59 percent of respondents favoring price caps.

The Republican response has bounced between pathetic and ignorant. The party cannot even pass a price transparency bill. Practically every other product and service in America comes with a price tag up front. Only medical care routinely hides prices until after the consumer uses it. Even for the most non-interventionist free marketer, this should be unacceptable. Price discovery is a fundamental underpinning of any functioning market.

Price discovery is not a magic bullet for reducing costs, but it is a step in the right direction. Yet the Republican Congress cannot even take that one step, and Trump seems totally uninterested. Price transparency should have passed last year, allowing Republicans to move forward with at least some basic administrative and bureaucratic reforms.

Instead, they have done nothing. The Republican Party has degenerated into a party focused on moaning rather than solving problems. If the midterms are a rout for the Democrats, they have only themselves to blame.

Keith Naughton is a former campaign consultant and co-founder of the public affairs firm Silent Majority Strategies. Find him on his Substack, “Betting On Politics.”

articles.title: The unifying pro-family policy hiding in plain sight
articles.summary: In a new national survey, 86 percent of Americans said mothers in the U.S. should not be dying from preventable causes in childbirth — a tragic reality that has worsened in recent years.
articles.body:
In Searcy County, Ark., a mother in labor faces an 84-minute drive to the nearest delivery room. One of the state’s most recent labor-and-delivery closures didn’t happen because a hospital ran out of money; it happened because its only OB-GYN died , and there was no one left to replace him.

Ask Americans, whether in red states, blue states or purple states, whether that’s acceptable, and you will find something rare in this country: agreement.

We know because we asked. In a new national survey , 86 percent of Americans said mothers in the U.S. should not be dying from preventable causes in childbirth — a tragic reality that has worsened in recent years . Each of the 15 policy solutions we tested won majority support. Thirteen cleared 80 percent.

The most popular fix , according to the 1,000 voters surveyed nationwide, is expanding telehealth and specialty care for rural and high-risk pregnancies — care that sends the specialist to the mother instead of asking her to make the drive. Large majorities also said insurance coverage should extend through every baby’s full first year, not stop at six weeks .

And by wide margins, Americans said they’d favor a political candidate who makes this a priority.

We are both moms. One of us has built a national campaign to make America the safest place in the world to have a baby. The other has spent decades as a political strategist and presidential counselor, testing and polling American sentiment on nearly every issue imaginable.

Ask Americans nuanced questions about immigration, education, the economy, foreign policy or almost anything else on the ballot this year and the country fractures, with many voters assuming the red or blue uniform. The issue of healthy moms and healthy babies lands differently.

What is most striking is how fast minds have moved. Before hearing a single fact about maternal mortality in America, 77 percent already wanted the system to improve. After hearing a just few statistics, that number rose to 86. What moved people most was learning that two-thirds of maternal deaths in the U.S. occur in the year after delivery, exactly when everyone assumes the danger has passed. Tell people that, and they stop debating; instead, they start asking why nobody told them sooner.

There is a reason the facts move people this fast. America now holds the record as the only wealthy nation where the risk of dying from a pregnancy-related cause has gone up , not down, over the last 40 years. The U.S. now ranks behind Russia and Ukraine on this key metric. Statistically, a mother is safer giving birth in a war-addled nation than she is here. We outspend the world on childbirth , but we don’t outperform.

The same logic holds after the baby is born. A nurse checking on a new mother within two weeks can catch a hemorrhage, an infection or a dangerous blood pressure spike before it becomes an emergency.

We require a car seat before a newborn can leave the hospital; we can do better than sending the mother home with an “Attagirl!” and a six-week follow-up. None of this is complicated. It is care that shows up where danger lurks.

So here is what we would ask: We urge the Senate to pass the Rural Obstetrics Readiness Act and the NIH Improve Act .

The first — from Sens. Maggie Hassan (D-N.H.), Susan Collins (R-Maine), Katie Britt (R-Ala.) and Tina Smith (D-Minn.) — trains and equips rural emergency rooms that have no labor-and-delivery unit to handle an obstetric emergency and puts a maternal health specialist on the line when a delivery goes wrong. It cleared the Senate Health Committee unanimously in July.

The second, led by Britt and Sen. Cory Booker (R-N.J.) with Reps. Lauren Underwood (D-Ill.) and Brian Fitzpatrick (R-Pa.) , guarantees steady funding for the National Institutes of Health research initiative already working to answer why American mothers are dying. The House passed it unanimously in July.

Neither bill is controversial. Both are sitting still.

We don’t need to persuade the public. They already agree. Now policymakers in Washington must act.

If you agree with 86 percent of the country, don’t just nod along. Call your senators. Ask them when they are voting. Healthy moms build healthy families, and healthy families build a stronger country. Americans already know that. Washington just needs to catch up.

Olivia Walton is the founder of Healthy Moms, Healthy Babies America , a bipartisan national campaign working to cut the U.S. maternal mortality rate in half within five years. Kellyanne Conway is the former senior counselor to President Trump and the founder of KAConsulting LLC , which conducted the polling referenced in this piece.

articles.title: Congressional staffers planned bipartisan trip with luxury stops in Europe ahead of election
articles.summary: A senior House aide was set to lead congressional staffers on an official trip to Europe featuring stops at a Ferrari factory, luxury goods companies and France’s Champagne region before Speaker Mike Johnson’s (R-La.) office abruptly canceled the plans. The weeklong trip to Italy and France, scheduled for later this month with the midterms just…
articles.body:
A senior House aide was set to lead congressional staffers on an official trip to Europe featuring stops at a Ferrari factory, luxury goods companies and France’s Champagne region before Speaker Mike Johnson’s (R-La.) office abruptly canceled the plans.

The weeklong trip to Italy and France, scheduled for later this month with the midterms just weeks away , was organized as a fact-finding mission to examine the effects of the Trump administration’s tariffs and taxes, NBC News reported Wednesday, citing a draft itinerary.

Following the outlet’s inquiries about the trip, Johnson’s office abruptly canceled it, citing a scheduling conflict.

Curt Beaulieu, Johnson’s senior policy and tax adviser, was tapped to lead the delegation, which was expected to include senior congressional staff from both parties.

The draft schedule showed the group beginning the swing in Vicenza, Italy, where staffers were slated to meet with U.S. military personnel stationed there. From there, the itinerary turned to industries caught up in President Trump’s trade agenda, according to the memo obtained by NBC.

“The purpose of the trip is to engage European and U.S. government and industry officials related to the impact of U.S. tariffs and taxes,” it reads.

The official congressional and staff delegations, also known as CODELs and STAFFDELs, are professional trips made by members of both parties or their staff to meet with global leaders or advocates to better understand a number of issues and build stronger ties.

The delegation planned to tour a Ferrari factory near Bologna, Italy, and a Barilla facility in Parma before heading to Milan or Florence to meet with luxury goods companies. In France, staffers were slated to visit the Champagne region to meet with the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development for talks on taxes and trade.

Johnson’s office told NBC that Michelin, L’Oreal Paris and drugmaker Sanofi were also among the companies considered for the itinerary. It also defended the proposed travel, saying congressional staff from both parties routinely visit U.S. allies and trading partners to meet with government and industry officials.

The proposed trip comes as Trump’s tariffs remain at the center of a broader debate over prices and trade ahead of November’s elections.

The president earlier this year threatened a 200 percent tariff on Champagne from France after French President Emmanuel Macron refused an invite to join the White House Board of Peace , which is overseeing the 20-point recovery plan in Gaza amid the Israel-Hamas ceasefire .

articles.title: Democrats call for Pulte resignation over FHFA watchdog budget cuts
articles.summary: Top Democratic lawmakers are calling on Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) Director Bill Pulte to resign after the agency cut funding for its inspector general, a move they say could effectively shut down the independent watchdog. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), along with several top Democrats including…
articles.body:
Top Democratic lawmakers are calling on Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) Director Bill Pulte to resign after the agency cut funding for its inspector general, a move they say could effectively shut down the independent watchdog.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), along with several top Democrats including Sen. Elizabeth Warren (Mass.), accused Pulte on Wednesday of trying to dismantle the office responsible for independently investigating fraud, waste and misconduct at the housing regulator.

“Bill Pulte is shutting down the independent watchdog that is responsible for investigating his misconduct — like his efforts to weaponize private mortgage data in sham investigations against the President’s perceived political enemies,” the lawmakers said in a joint statement released Wednesday night.

“Pulte’s corrupt crusade to protect himself and President Trump from accountability will likely result in the firing of approximately 40 law enforcement personnel who protect families from mortgage fraud,” the statement continued. “Bill Pulte should resign, and if he does not, Congress must hold him accountable.”

FHFA announced the cuts in a press release Wednesday, arguing that the inspector general’s budget and staffing levels were far higher than those of watchdogs at other federal agencies.

The inspector general had requested a budget equal to 16 percent of FHFA’s operating budget, according to the agency. FHFA said inspectors general across the federal government receive an average of about 2 percent of their agencies’ budgets.

The watchdog’s employees also make up 18 percent of FHFA’s workforce, compared with an average of about 4 percent at other agencies, FHFA said.

“FHFA cannot justify such a discrepancy to the American people,” the agency said, adding that it “fully supports the independence and mission” of the inspector general.

Pulte responded on the social platform X by firing back at Warren, referring to her by a derogatory nickname and accusing her of wanting to “waste precious federal money like a drunken sailor.”

The agency’s inspector general position has been vacant since last year after Reuters reported the ouster of acting Inspector General Joe Allen.

articles.title: House Democrats call for GAO to investigate government-funded Trump ads
articles.summary: A pair of House Democrats called on the U.S. Government Accountability Office (GAO) to investigate government-funded ads featuring President Trump that aired last month. Reps. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.), ranking member of the House Judiciary Committee, and George Whitesides (D-Calif.) sent a letter to the GAO leadership asking for an investigation into why “the American people…
articles.body:
A pair of House Democrats called on the U.S. Government Accountability Office (GAO) to investigate government-funded ads featuring President Trump that aired last month.

Reps. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.), ranking member of the House Judiciary Committee, and George Whitesides (D-Calif.) sent a letter to the GAO leadership asking for an investigation into why “the American people are apparently paying for Donald Trump to create desperate preelection propaganda.”

“These ads constitute an illegal use of taxpayer funds, perhaps best demonstrated by the fact that they are virtually identical to the ones Donald Trump used during his 2024 presidential campaign, and in fact use the same footage and the same inept ideological messaging,” the lawmakers continued.

The letter accused Trump of violating multiple federal laws by using taxpayer money to fund the TV ads — including the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2026 , which states that no appropriated funds may be used “for publicity or propaganda purposes within the United States” unless authorized by Congress.

They also cited the Antideficiency Act and other federal criminal statutes.

Raskin and Whitesides concluded in their letter that the GAO has “an important responsibility to hold accountable members of his Administration who violate the laws and policies under your purview.”

A GAO spokesperson told The Hill it had received the congressional request, saying, “GAO has a process it goes through to determine whether we do work and when, which we are working through right now.”

The federal government released multiple ads last month centering on different points in the Trump agenda. The White House has labeled the ads as “public service announcements.” The ad’s disclaimer reads, “Paid for by the U.S. Government.”

When asked about the ad campaign, Trump told reporters , “I’m not running for office, first of all.”

“When I’m talking about making America great, making our country great, that’s a countrywide ad. That’s an ad for the spirit of our country,” the president said.

Federal Communications Commission head Brendan Carr said the ad struck him as “normal course public service announcements that you see all the time,” adding that it does not warrant any review by the agency.

The ad campaign has received criticism from Republicans in the upper chamber as well.

“It’s a great message. I like the message, but it shouldn’t be paid for by taxpayer dollars,” Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) told reporters Monday.

articles.title: Trump not ruling out invoking Insurrection Act around midterms
articles.summary: President Trump said in an interview published Thursday that he has not ruled out invoking the Insurrection Act or declaring a national emergency around the midterm elections in November. “I’m not committing to anything,” Trump said in an interview with Time when asked about the limits of his presidential power. “We’re going to see how…
articles.body:
President Trump said in an interview published Thursday that he has not ruled out invoking the Insurrection Act or declaring a national emergency around the midterm elections in November.

“I’m not committing to anything,” Trump said in an interview with Time when asked about the limits of his presidential power. “We’re going to see how it plays out in court.”

The outlet reported that White House advisers have already thought about how to respond if Democrats reclaim either or both the House and the Senate. One official said the administration will “be forced to think more bipartisan.”

“I would hope that if we win, we can still do that, because for two years we’ve run a completely partisan play,” the official told Time. “When you’re looking back on your time, I don’t think that’s what you should be proud of, even if it was successful.”

Trump, however, has warned that if Democrats reclaim either chamber, they will attempt to impeach him for a third time. He dismissed unfavorable polling for him and other Republicans as being fake.

The president has a history of threatening to deploy troops via the Insurrection Act of 1807 between his two terms. He threatened to send troops to Minneapolis after an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer shot and killed U.S. citizen Renee Good in January, before saying there was no reason to invoke the law.

In June 2025, he said he would “certainly” invoke the act in response to anti-ICE demonstrations in the streets of Los Angeles, and he said so again about similar protests in Portland, Ore., in October. He likened both situations to “insurrections.”

Trump also said he considered sending troops to Minneapolis late in his first term after protests erupted following the murder of George Floyd by police in 2020.

The law’s history is tied to possible violence riled up by a former vice president, as former President Thomas Jefferson sought to confront former Vice President Aaron Burr’s organized venture to establish a new country in the Louisiana Territory in 1807, according to the National Constitution Center . The Insurrection Act became law after Burr was arrested in Alabama and charged with treason.

The act allows the president “in all cases of insurrection, or obstruction to the laws, either of the United States, or of any individual state or territory,” to deploy members of the military or federalize members of a state’s National Guard “for the purpose of suppressing such insurrection, or of causing the laws to be duly executed.”

Trump has relied on Title 10 to send federal troops to U.S. cities. Title 10 is a federal code that gives the president the authority to deploy the National Guard to assist local law enforcement in a supporting function.

The Insurrection Act was last invoked by former President George H.W. Bush in May 1992, in response to the Los Angeles riots, after four Los Angeles Police Department officers were acquitted of beating Rodney King, a flash point in the city’s history that was captured on videotape. Fifteen U.S. presidents have invoked it.

articles.title: Maryland Democrats should reject gerrymandering and set a national precedent
articles.summary: Marylanders have a chance in November to turn the tide against one of the worst tactics in American politics.
articles.body:
The mid-decade redistricting initiated by President Trump is mostly finished for the moment, except in Maryland. In November, voters across the state will be asked to support or oppose Question Three, a constitutional amendment that would pave the way for additional gerrymandering. The phrasing of the question makes it difficult to understand its intended purpose, but it seeks to remove any requirement that congressional districts be compact, contiguous and respectful of geographic features.

This means that Cumberland in Western Maryland and Salisbury on the Eastern Shore — separated by the Chesapeake Bay and nearly the entire width of the state — could one day end up represented by the same member of Congress. Maryland could end up with polka-dot districts, where neighborhoods in distant cities and rural counties are joined together with narrow tendrils to create a favorable mix of voters.

Democratic voters in Maryland are being told by Gov. Wes Moore (D) and his allies in the legislature that a vote in favor of Question Three is a way to fight back against President Trump. Their argument is undermined, however, by the reality that Democrats have been trying to gerrymander Maryland’s last Republican held district out of existence for many years, including as recently as 2022 when Trump was out of office and Joe Biden was president.

Maryland Democrats are being offered a false choice. It is simply not necessary to gerrymander Maryland to oppose Trump. Despite what Marylanders are being told, adopting tactics we abhor makes our politics worse instead of better. Democrats are on track to retake control of the House in November and are competing well in Senate races that seemed out of reach until recently. The Democratic control of Congress after November’s election does not at all depend on Maryland gerrymandering.

The earliest Democrats could enact new maps would be for the 2028 election . These new maps would make it difficult for Republicans to hold the 1st Congressional District. Maryland would probably send eight Democrats to the House and no Republicans.

This gerrymandered result would net Democrats one extra seat in Congress. Maryland’s all-Democratic delegation would be sworn in on Jan. 3, 2029, just 17 days before President Trump leaves office and two years after Democrats likely take control of the House. Despite Moore’s assurances to the contrary, it is not necessary for Maryland to undertake another round of gerrymandering for Democrats to stand up to the president.

Marylanders could be forgiven for believing the tide is running in favor of gerrymandering, but there are encouraging signs that the worst is over, and a better approach can prevail.

In Indiana, Republican State Senate President Pro Tem Rodric Bray and 20 of his Republican colleagues defied President Trump and refused to support pro-Republican gerrymandering. Bray and others understood they would pay a heavy political price for their actions, but this didn’t stop them from doing what was right. More recently, the Supreme Court blocked an effort to use Missouri’s new Republican-gerrymandered map in the 2026 election, leaving in place the map from 2022, drawn before this year’s frenzy of redistricting.

As bad as gerrymandering is elsewhere, Question Three in Maryland seeks an even worse outcome. Unlike Texas, which will still send some Democrats to Congress even after redistricting, or California, which returns power to an independent districting commission in 2030, Democrats in Maryland are seeking to entirely eliminate Republicans from the state’s congressional delegation and change the constitution , almost certainly guaranteeing the legality of gerrymandering in Maryland long into the future.

Maryland’s Democratic voters are being told by their leaders that the way to fight fire is with fire. In fact, the way to fight fire is to put out the flame. Large numbers of Maryland voters already understand this, and only 28 percent of them in a bipartisan poll are ready to support Question Three. A second poll by a Democratic firm without Republican input found that 40 percent of Marylanders were in favor of the question, still well below the threshold for passage.

Most Marylanders know that gerrymandering is wrong, and both polls show a majority of voters aren’t ready to emulate the bad behavior of other states and embrace gerrymandering. Marylanders have a chance in November to turn the tide against one of the worst tactics in American politics. This would have national implications. Rejecting Question Three would send a powerful signal that not every American is ready to succumb to cynicism and propagate the worst parts of our political culture.

After a year of mid-decade redistricting, few states can command the moral high ground on the issue. By rejecting Question Three, Maryland would be different. An overwhelmingly Democratic state that pushed back against its Democratic leaders as they tried to gerrymander Maryland’s last Republican congressional seat out of existence would be an extraordinary development. With its honor intact, Maryland can then help push the nation toward a more representative and productive version of politics.

Colin Pascal is a retired Army lieutenant colonel, a registered Democrat and a founding member of the nonpartisan group Protect Maryland Votes, an organization opposed to gerrymandering and Question Three.

articles.title: Christa Pike: Timeline of botched Tennessee execution
articles.summary: The state of Tennessee failed to put Christa Pike to death Wednesday after two doses of a lethal drug were administered following a stay granted by a lower court before the Supreme Court allowed the execution to proceed.
articles.body:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. ( WKRN ) — The state of Tennessee failed to put Christa Pike to death Wednesday after two doses of a lethal drug were administered following a stay granted by a lower court before the Supreme Court allowed the execution to proceed.

According to media witnesses, Pike, 50, was alive and snoring when they were escorted from the death chamber. She was taken from Riverbend Maximum Security Prison in an ambulance to a Nashville-area hospital, where her condition is unknown.

Pike was given two doses of pentobarbital. Her attorneys released the following statement:

Tonight the State of Tennessee once again failed to carry out a lawful execution. We take no pleasure in being right, but the concerns raised by Ms. Pike proved to be true: difficult vein access, blown veins, degraded pentobarbital, no emergency medical care available when things inevitably go wrong, all under a protocol that remains veiled in secrecy. Randy Spivey and Kelly Gleason from the TN Office of the Post Conviction Defender, and Stephen Ferrell and Luke Ihnen from Federal Defender Services of Eastern Tennessee

Tonight the State of Tennessee once again failed to carry out a lawful execution. We take no pleasure in being right, but the concerns raised by Ms. Pike proved to be true: difficult vein access, blown veins, degraded pentobarbital, no emergency medical care available when things inevitably go wrong, all under a protocol that remains veiled in secrecy.

Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee (R) has delayed the remaining execution this year for Gary Wayne Sutton, who was scheduled to be put to death on Dec. 3.

Journalists from local media outlets who were selected to watch the execution spent all day at the prison. They provided a comprehensive timeline of the execution once they were released.

6:41 p.m. Media witnesses were let into the observation room next to the death chamber. They were allowed to hear what happened in the room through a microphone system.

7:15 p.m. Witnesses who have previously watched executions noted it was taking longer than normal to begin.

7:27 p.m. Curtains to the execution chamber were raised and Pike was strapped to a gurney with an IV in her right arm.

Pike gave her last words and began to sing with her spiritual advisor while he patted her head, and they exchanged words.

7:31 p.m. Pike said, “The vein in my arm feels like it’s about to bust,” and asked her spiritual advisor if this is normal.

7:34 p.m. Pike asked her spiritual advisor to tell someone she loves him.

7:41 p.m. The rock was placed in the observation window for the first time.

The significance of the rock is not exactly known, but it is believed to signal that the lethal drug has been administered and the waiting process has begun.

7:43 p.m. Pike was seen grinding her jaw.

7:44 p.m. Pike took a deep breath and continued to speak.

7:46 p.m. The curtains are closed for the first time.

7:49 p.m. The curtains are reopened and Pike is seen with her mouth open. She can be heard snoring by the witnesses. Her spiritual advisor, who had been removed from the room, was ushered back inside.

7:51 p.m. Choking sounds can be heard along with more snoring. Alarms believed to be from dying batteries of TDOC employees can be heard.

7:54 p.m. Pike grunted, lifted her head and continued snoring.

7:56 p.m. Pike lifted off the gurney so her body made a V shape.

8 p.m. Faint sounds of breathing were heard.

8:01 p.m. The rock was placed in the window for a second time.

8:02 p.m. Louder snoring was heard from Pike.

8:05 p.m. The curtains are closed for a final time. Witnesses asked repeatedly if the curtains could be reopened since Pike could still be heard snoring.

8:53 p.m. The microphone was cut off after the warden asked the witnesses to exit the area.

Pike was scheduled to be executed at 9 a.m. Wednesday, before the Sixth Circuit Court of Appeals approved a last-minute request for a stay of execution.

The Tennessee Attorney General’s Office appealed to the Supreme Court, which allowed the execution to proceed.

Pike was convicted of brutally killing 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer in Knoxville in 1995 when she was 18. She would have been the first woman put to death in Tennessee in more than 200 years.

Prosecutors said Slemmer was lured into a wooded area before being tortured and killed by Pike and her then-boyfriend in 1995. Pike told prosecutors she believed Slemmer was trying to steal her boyfriend.

“Carrying out a lawfully imposed sentence is among the State’s most serious responsibilities, and the people of Tennessee expect it to be done in a manner that is not only legal and constitutional, but is effective. I have ordered a comprehensive, third-party review to determine exactly what occurred. Therefore, the remaining scheduled execution will not be carried out this year.”

The Tennessee Department of Correction also issued a statement hours after the failed execution attempt:

“ The Tennessee Department of Correction followed every step of the State’s lawful, established execution protocol approved by the Attorney General’s Office. The lethal injection chemical in the protocol has consistently been effective, and the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out this evening. Christa Pike has been transported to an off-site medical facility. “

Tennessee’s execution protocol calls for a second set of syringes to be administered “if the inmate is not deceased” after the first.

Seven people have survived medical problems due to an execution team’s failure to access a vein to administer lethal injection drugs, but no one has stayed alive after receiving the drugs used in such executions, according to the Associated Press.

This is the second time in 2026 Tennessee has been unable to carry out an execution: In May, state officials called off the execution of Tony Carruthers after executioners failed to place an IV to administer the lethal injection.

Since the Supreme Court reinstated the death penalty in 1976, 18 women have been put to death, representing about 1 percent of all executions, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.

Pike would have been the 30th person executed in the U.S. this year.

Tennessee announced in 2024 it was switching from a three-drug series for lethal injections to the single drug pentobarbital. That came more than two years after Tennessee abruptly halted the execution of Oscar Smith and acknowledged it had failed to ensure its lethal injection drugs were tested properly.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: Trump says he regrets nominating Gorsuch, Kavanaugh and Barrett
articles.summary: President Trump revealed in an interview published Thursday that he regrets nominating conservative Justices Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh, and Amy Coney Barrett to the Supreme Court. “Yeah. Yeah. What can I do? I put them in,” Trump told Time magazine when asked whether he regretted nominating the three justices to the high court. “They voted…
articles.body:
President Trump revealed in an interview published Thursday that he regrets nominating conservative Justices Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh, and Amy Coney Barrett to the Supreme Court.

“Yeah. Yeah. What can I do? I put them in,” Trump told Time magazine when asked whether he regretted nominating the three justices to the high court.

“They voted against me too often,” the president continued. “I gave them the position of a lifetime, and they vote against me often. They vote for me too.”

Trump went on to note how Democrats “stick like glue” when they vote, saying he admires the party’s loyalty to their leaders.

“So they have loyalty to Barack Hussein Obama. They have loyalty to Biden, even though Biden doesn’t even know who the hell they are. He wouldn’t know. He doesn’t even know what the Supreme Court is. And me, I gave them the chance of a lifetime, and it’s unfortunate what they did,” he said.

When asked if he wants loyalty from his Supreme Court picks, Trump said he wants “good decisions.”

“The tariff decision was disastrous for the country. I want good decisions for the country,” Trump said.

The president also railed against the high court’s decision to strike down his executive order on birthright citizenship .

The president’s latest comments come after he criticized the three justices for voting with the majority of the court to block his mail-in voting plan last month.

“These are not the people I interviewed to serve on the United States Supreme Court, they are merely a shell of their original selves,” he wrote in a Truth Social post.

In February, the high court struck down the bulk of his tariffs in a 6-3 decision by rejecting his expanded use of the International Emergency Economic Powers Act in imposing tariffs on nearly every country.

In another 6-3 decision, the high court ruled against Trump’s birthright citizenship ban in June, upholding the guarantees in the 14th Amendment.

Coney Barrett ruled against the administration in both decisions, while Gorsuch ruled to strike down his tariffs and Kavanaugh ruled to strike down his birthright citizenship move.

articles.title: MAHA’s not buying what AOC is selling
articles.summary: Tony Lyons, longtime friend of Kennedy Jr., and president of the nonprofit MAHA Action, told me Ocasio-Cortez’s motivations are purely political and not substantive.
articles.body:
To paraphrase Shakespeare’s “ The Tempest ,” misery makes strange bedfellows. But such bedfellows are essential for solutions in the case of chronic childhood illness, which affects 40 percent of U.S. children, and obesity, which affects approximately 20 percent of children.

When I interviewed Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. at the Environmental Protection Agency recently, he suggested that bipartisan congressional legislation is needed in order to repeal a loophole tied to dangerous food additives designated with the “ generally recognized as safe ” status under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act .

It is a ridiculous blind spot in federal law which, since 1958 , has allowed Big Food to “ self-affirm ” that preservatives, colorings and other chemicals added to our food supply are safe for consumption. A bipartisan law is needed to close it and restore common sense.

What about Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.)? She, too, has long been an opponent of toxic chemicals in the environment. She co-sponsored legislation targeting “ forever chemicals ” in water that impair fertility and are associated with immune dysfunction and cancer. She has also secured funding for access to healthy, unprocessed food .

Last month, she reached out to Make America Healthy Again organizers and met with Zen Honeycutt of Moms Across America and Joe Maxwell of Farm Action. But Tony Lyons, longtime friend of Kennedy Jr., and president of the nonprofit MAHA Action, told me Ocasio-Cortez’s motivations are purely political and not substantive.

“She says she wants to fight Big Food, Big Pharma, Big Ag,” he began. “Sounds like Secretary Kennedy. [She] says she wants to protect families, yet she criticizes all the time the very person Trump brought in to fight government agencies because they are harming the public.”

He said Ocasio-Cortez “should want all these products to get better and safer,” but is “inconsistent” because she is unwilling to defend Kennedy’s work to close the loophole.

“If she really wanted to defend children and working families, she would be on board with the whole MAHA agenda. If 60 percent have chronic disease, if she is against poverty, then she has to work with Kennedy and Trump and not only hyper focus on one person dying of measles while saying nothing about 1.2 million people dying each year from preventable chronic disease.”

“The midterms are about MAHA,” Lyons added. “She can’t get on the MAHA train after blasting and slashing everything Kennedy and Trump represent.” When it comes to the weed-killer glyphosate, an herbicide many health activists say is not safe for the food supply, Lyons says there must be concrete steps on safety.

“We need warnings on packages, to encourage innovation [and] no liability shields while working with farmers to engage in regenerative farming which doesn’t rely on pesticides,” he said. “We need to change the culture.”

Ocasio-Cortez “says she wants to build a new world, a better future, where we guarantee the dignity of all of our people,” and Kennedy Jr. “is fighting every day in the trenches to create that world,” he said.

To be fair, Ocasio-Cortez has championed farm-to-table supply chains through the GrowNYC’s Regional Food Hub , has tried to help overcome food deserts and supported food rescue campaigns through City Harvest with the goal of universal access to healthy food.

But MAHA accomplishments have been far greater and have included securing pledges from Big Food to phase out petroleum-based artificial food dyes, enabling state-wide Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program waivers to restrict junk food purchases and pushing to improve the nutritional quality of food served in schools and public facilities.

“If you want a better world with more dignity, then you should want to line up with Kennedy in the fight against chronic disease,” Lyons said. “Anything else is just politics and pandering and disingenuous. And voters can see right through it.”

Marc Siegel MD is a clinical professor of medicine and medical director of Doctor Radio at NYU Langone Health. He is the author of the upcoming book, The Angels Among Us.

articles.title: Rubio ordered Iranians out of US as negotiations stalled
articles.summary: Secretary of State Marco Rubio ordered the Iranian delegation to leave the U.S. immediately Monday after the United Nations General Assembly as negotiations between both countries have stalled. The Hill’s broadcast partner NewsNation on Thursday confirmed this with the State Department, which previously approved visas for the “core” Iranian delegation to the U.N. last month.…
articles.body:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio ordered the Iranian delegation to leave the U.S. immediately Monday after the United Nations General Assembly as negotiations between both countries have stalled.

The Hill’s broadcast partner NewsNation on Thursday confirmed this with the State Department, which previously approved visas for the “core” Iranian delegation to the U.N. last month.

Rubio lost patience with the Iranian officials Monday and said Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and his delegation should immediately leave, The Associated Press reported , citing two officials familiar with the order.

One official told the outlet that Rubio determined that the delegates “overstayed their welcome” and should depart given high-level meetings have concluded.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian left New York City the day after he spoke before the U.N. General Assembly last week, but Araghchi stayed behind for indirect talks with the U.S., the AP reported. He planned to stay in the Big Apple until Wednesday.

Araghchi and his team left very early Tuesday, but the delegation denied being ordered to leave.

“The Iranian delegation left New York on Monday evening, in accordance with the schedule that had also been communicated to the U.S. Department of State in advance on September 17,” the delegation stated on the social platform X . “Having achieved nothing, the State Department has resorted to propagating baseless and worthless news.”

The U.S.-Israeli conflict in Iran stretched to its seven-month mark Monday, with both countries negotiating through intermediaries. Pezeshkian and President Trump have said they are looking for a deal, although the U.S. president rejected a peace proposal from Iran that would reopen the Strait of Hormuz and enact a ceasefire.

Iranian government spokesperson Fatemeh Mohajerani said Wednesday that negotiators received an official U.S. response to the proposal, though no other details were offered.

Critics in the U.S. against the regime have accused it of dragging out the conflict and talks with the U.S. to have it hamper Trump’s policies toward Iran after the midterms. An Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps spokesperson, Gen. Hossein Mohebbi, earlier this week urged American voters to rally against Trump so as to change U.S. policy toward Tehran.

“Although American politicians often win your votes through deception and false promises, as Trump did, you can change the makeup of the government if you apply the criteria for good leadership in choosing the people you vote into office,” Mohebbi said in a letter to voters obtained by The Times of Israel .

The conflict’s unpopularity, with its effect on rising prices and the soaring cost of gasoline and diesel , has put pressure on GOP campaigns where Republicans are seeking to distance themselves from the president and calling for the war to end, as well as requesting that the U.S. lift its naval blockade off Iranian ports.

Some of those supporting the administration’s efforts against the regime have said that Iran is looking to drag out talks with the U.S. to damage Trump politically .

articles.title: Jennings on Paxton comments about Trump convention: ‘Keep it to yourself’
articles.summary: Conservative commentator Scott Jennings went after Texas Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton on Wednesday over the latter’s comments about the Republican midterm convention in Dallas. “Ken Paxton has an excellent chance to win, and he needs Donald Trump’s help, and he needs Donald Trump’s voters to do that. And mostly, they need Donald Trump and…
articles.body:
Conservative commentator Scott Jennings went after Texas Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton on Wednesday over the latter’s comments about the Republican midterm convention in Dallas.

“Ken Paxton has an excellent chance to win, and he needs Donald Trump’s help, and he needs Donald Trump’s voters to do that. And mostly, they need Donald Trump and the Republican Party’s resources because he obviously isn’t the fundraiser that [James] Talarico is in this race,” Jennings said on “CNN NewsNight.”

“So, for a lot of reasons, I was not happy with this comment today from Ken Paxton. Even if he thinks he was being honest, sometimes, keep it to yourself and say, ‘We’re grateful for everyone’s support,’” he added.

Paxton, the Texas attorney general, said the Republican midterm convention in Dallas was a political negative for him.

“So to be honest with you, the numbers — when we did that convention — it dropped our numbers. Everybody’s numbers dropped. Right now, yeah, not good,” Paxton said in an audio clip The New York Times shared Wednesday. The Texas Republican had been asked if he thought that “he’s a little bit of a drag,” though it was not clear who the person asking the question was referencing.

The Times reported that Paxton’s comment came at a private fundraiser with conservative donors and lobbyists in Washington.

Senior Paxton adviser Nick Maddux told The Hill that “this is more manipulated nonsense from The New York Times to create a story that doesn’t exist.”

Paxton is facing a competitive race for Texas Senate in a state that usually leans Republican. However, the electoral environment for GOP candidates is not favorable as they head into the midterms, with Trump’s approval rating slumping, the unpopular war in Iran and widespread concerns about the economy.

The Hill has reached out to Paxton’s campaign for comment.

articles.title: Appeals court rules Trump’s name can’t be carved into Institute of Peace building
articles.summary: A federal appeals court on Wednesday night ruled that President Trump’s name can’t be carved into the U.S. Institute of Peace building, for now. The judges are considering a lawsuit brought by removed board members, who challenge the administration’s takeover of the institute. The appeals court has allowed the takeover to proceed until it resolves the case. Trump’s name now appears on…
articles.body:
A federal appeals court on Wednesday night ruled that President Trump’s name can’t be carved into the U.S. Institute of Peace building, for now.

The judges are considering a lawsuit brought by removed board members , who challenge the administration’s takeover of the institute. The appeals court has allowed the takeover to proceed until it resolves the case.

Trump’s name now appears on signage outside the institute’s headquarters in the nation’s capital, and last month, the former members headed back to court over concerns the administration intended to permanently carve it into the building’s facade.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit agreed to block any plans to move it forward in a one-sentence order without explanation. It remains in effect until the court issues its final ruling. Oral arguments are scheduled for November.

The former board members said the building is a “work of expressive architecture,” and Trump’s name shouldn’t be so easily etched into it until the litigation is resolved.

“Alteration of the design to impose a different message would cause irreparable harm,” their attorneys wrote in court filings.

The former board members originally filed the lawsuit in March 2025 after Trump removed them. It’s one of many agencies across the federal bureaucracy that Trump has targeted since retaking the White House.

A federal district judge agreed the firings were without legal authority and the takeover wasn’t allowed, but the D.C. Circuit put that ruling on hold as it considers the case. It’s now weighing the impact of the Supreme Court’s blockbuster decision eviscerating independent agency removal protections, which could further bolster Trump’s position.

The Justice Department told the D.C. Circuit to deny the former board members’ request in light of that.

It also insisted that there were no imminent plans to carve Trump’s name into the building and that the State Department had merely done “preparatory market research” for the project, including contacting vendors and getting estimates.

“However, the Department has authorized us to state that it did not take further action with awards or selecting a vendor for any engraving since that time and has no current plans to move forward with engraving the building or retaining wall,” the Justice Department wrote in court filings on Monday.

articles.title: Van Orden hit with cease and desist letter from Democratic opponent over AI deepfake ads
articles.summary: Rep. Derrick Van Orden (R-Wis.) was hit with a cease and desist letter from his Democratic opponent, Rebecca Cooke, after the lawmaker aired AI deepfake campaign advertisements about her. “Not only are these ads beneath the dignity of your office, but Wisconsin’s common law of defamation fills the gaps yet remaining in Wisconsin’s statutory protections…
articles.body:
Rep. Derrick Van Orden (R-Wis.) was hit with a cease and desist letter from his Democratic opponent , Rebecca Cooke, after the lawmaker aired AI deepfake campaign advertisements about her.

“Not only are these ads beneath the dignity of your office, but Wisconsin’s common law of defamation fills the gaps yet remaining in Wisconsin’s statutory protections against fake AI videos,” reads the letter, which Cooke shared on social media.

Cooke’s lawyer wrote the videos “undermine our democratic process” and said it was “the exact kind of mudslinging voters are tired of.”

“You are indisputably posting videos falsely conveying that Ms. Cooke has made particular statements,” the letter continued, accusing Van Orden’s campaign of airing the ads “for the patently obvious purpose of harming Ms. Cooke’s reputation for your own political advantage.”

Van Orden responded to Cooke’s letter on social media with another AI-generated deepfake video of his Democratic opponent as a red bird with a Democratic Socialists of America shirt. His other ads targeted Cooke’s financial disclosures , which revealed that she earned additional income on top of her waitress salary as a political consultant.

“Rebecca Cooke is embarrassing herself because she got busted lying again and is now trying to cover it up,” Van Orden’s campaign wrote in a statement to local outlet WEAU . “The only thing Cooke is really concerned about is that people are finally getting to see her for what she is: an untrustworthy political hack who is willing to say or do anything for power.”

It is unclear whether Van Orden violated Wisconsin defamation statutes , which make it illegal for any person “with knowledge that it is false” to publicize “any false and unauthorized advertisement.”

The race between Van Orden and Cooke has been classified as a “toss-up” House seat in central and western Wisconsin, according to Cook Political Report .

Cooke lost to Van Orden in 2024 by just more than 11,000 votes, but Democrats targeted a new angle: the lawmaker’s ties to President Trump. Trump’s popularity slipped to its lowest point in September amid his ongoing tariff war with Canada, which is Wisconsin’s largest trading partner in 2025, according to the U.S. trade representative’s office .

Democrats have also targeted Van Orden’s appearance at Trump’s rally before the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol.

articles.title: Trump refuses to rule out demolishing Kennedy Center
articles.summary: President Trump is refusing to commit to not demolishing the Kennedy Center amid the legal battle over the performing arts center’s name and renovation. Trump, in a new interview with Time magazine, was asked if he would commit to not bringing in wrecking balls to take down the center without congressional consent. “I’m not committing…
articles.body:
President Trump is refusing to commit to not demolishing the Kennedy Center amid the legal battle over the performing arts center’s name and renovation .

Trump, in a new interview with Time magazine , was asked if he would commit to not bringing in wrecking balls to take down the center without congressional consent.

“I’m not committing to anything. We’re going to see how it plays out in court,” he said. “But if I build it, and if I agree that for the rest of my life, I’m going to be putting up $100 million to have it open to people … then I think the Trump administration should be recognized.”

The center’s board voted last month to immediately close the main building for renovations after officials indicated the center faces “certain fiscal collapse within weeks” and that it is “unsafe for continued occupancy.”

A decision from the D.C. Circuit is will determine if Trump’s name can be added to the building. It was added earlier this year but then removed after a court ruling.

Trump has since said renovations will not take place until the court rules on the center’s name change to include his name.

The president said in the Time interview that he’d be “willing to save it, but it’s in terrible, terrible shape.”

“Only I can save it, and I’ll tell you the biggest problem with the Kennedy Center — I can build it, but it will lose like many of those places,” he said. “If you look at Carnegie Hall, New York, and all these places, the artsy places, they lose tens of millions of dollars.”

He railed against the judge who ruled his name had to be taken off the building, calling him a “radical-left Trump hater.”

“Well, why would I want to stick with something that’s going to lose hundreds of millions of dollars, and I’m not even recognized?” he said. “It’s not me; it’s the administration.”

A recent letter from former Kennedy Center employees accused the center’s leadership of stopping planned waterproofing repairs earlier this year.

David Seide, an attorney representing the whistleblowers, said the center’s executive director, Matt Floca, had known about the issues “for years” but canceled the repairs despite the center receiving millions from Congress for its renovation.

“In sum, the evidence shows that the New Problems were in fact well known, were not considered to be high priorities and that millions in taxpayer funds were set aside more than a year ago to address them,” Seide wrote in the letter to Congress.

The letter also alleges Floca diverted the funds from Congress for repairs to make “unplanned cosmetic changes” requested by Trump to repaint the main building’s columns white last year.

Floca has pushed back on the allegations, saying “the safety of our patrons, artists, and staff comes first.”

“The Kennedy Center has known for years that the roof overhang leaked. What we did not know until this summer was how far the damage had spread inside it,” he said.

articles.title: Mountain-sized makeover: Hart Senate Building’s Calder sculpture getting newly restored mobile
articles.summary: A mountain-sized sculpture inside the Hart Senate Office Building is getting a major — and moving — cutting-edge upgrade. Mountains and Clouds, the massive installation by Alexander Calder that fills much of the building’s atrium, is undergoing a restoration effort that will include, for the first time, a mobile that will finally move in the…
articles.body:
A mountain-sized sculpture inside the Hart Senate Office Building is getting a major — and moving — cutting-edge upgrade.

Mountains and Clouds , the massive installation by Alexander Calder that fills much of the building’s atrium, is undergoing a restoration effort that will include, for the first time, a mobile that will finally move in the way that the famed artist intended. The restoration project was announced Thursday by the Calder Foundation.

Calder conceived the two-part “aesthetic equilibrium” sculpture shortly before his death in 1976. Mountain and Clouds made its debut inside the Hart building 10 years later.

The 51-foot-high grounded stabile is often viewed as the “mountains” of the sculpture, while the mobile, which spans 75 feet, is known as the “clouds.”

But according to Calder’s eponymous foundation, “due to the limits of engineering technology and available materials at that time,” the mobile component didn’t move how the sculptor originally had envisioned.

The mobile had frozen in place by 1992 before ultimately being deinstalled in 2014.

As part of the $12 million restoration effort, the mobile was rebuilt “employing new, cutting-edge advances in engineering and technology,” the Calder Foundation said.

“This restoration project will allow visitors from across the United States and around the world, as well as the Senators and staffers who work in Hart, to experience Mountains and Clouds as Calder envisioned, with the work’s mobile and stabile in poetic, dynamic dialogue,” a statement said.

The restoration, expected to be completed later this year, was part of a “historic public-private initiative” funded by philanthropists Jon and Kim Shirley, the foundation said, noting that the project “came at no cost to taxpayers.”

“With the mobile’s return, the atrium will once again serve as a living civic space where the public can encounter one of the great achievements of American art,” the nonprofit said.

Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle, many of whom championed the decadelong initiative, hailed the upgrade to the iconic multistory mobile inside Hart.

“Mountains and Clouds is an American work of art that has been a part of the Hart Building for four decades,” Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.) said.

“The restoration is a reminder of the importance of preserving the art and history of the U.S. Capitol,” Klobuchar said.

“The Hart Building belongs to the American people, and so does the art within it,” Sen. James Lankford (R-Okla.) said.

“With the restoration of Mountains and Clouds almost complete, every visitor, whether they’re here for a hearing, a tour, or simply passing through, will get to experience an icon of American art history,” he said.

“The work of Alexander Calder stands tall outside of my offices in both Washington and Chicago. But for too long, half of the story of Mountains and Clouds has been missing,” Sen. Dick Durbin (D-Ill.) said in a statement. Thanking the Shirleys and the Calder Foundation, he said that “this remarkable sculpture will once again be experienced by the public the way Alexander Calder intended.”

“When I became the chairman of the Rules Committee, my very first request from a colleague was, ‘Can we rehang the clouds?'” former Sen. Roy Blunt (R-Mo.) said.

“It has taken more than a decade, but the answer is yes,” Blunt said.

Soon, Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Conn.) said, “Americans from across the country traveling to the Senate will be greeted by this masterpiece in all its restored glory.”

“One of our nation’s most significant works of public art has stood incomplete for decades, right here in the U.S. Senate,” Sen. Angus King (I-Maine) said.

“I’m thrilled that the restoration of Alexander Calder’s Mountains and Clouds is moving forward,” King said, “and that the ‘Clouds’ have returned to Hart.”

articles.title: Supreme Court agrees to take up zoning dispute over Kentucky church shrine
articles.summary: A dispute over whether a local zoning ordinance in Kentucky that prohibited a Catholic church from building a religious shrine next to its property is legal is headed to the Supreme Court. The justices agreed Thursday to take up the request from Missionaries of St. John the Baptist, a church in the Cincinnati suburbs that…
articles.body:
A dispute over whether a local zoning ordinance in Kentucky that prohibited a Catholic church from building a religious shrine next to its property is legal is headed to the Supreme Court.

The justices agreed Thursday to take up the request from Missionaries of St. John the Baptist, a church in the Cincinnati suburbs that was denied a permit to construct a large grotto honoring the Virgin Mary in an adjacent lot.

At issue is whether that denial violates the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA), which is designed in part to protect against zoning laws that impose a “substantial burden” on religious exercise.

“Telling a church it can’t build a modest place for prayer and reflection on its own property is outrageous,” said Kelly Shackelford, the President, CEO and Chief Counsel at First Liberty, one of the groups representing the church. “Federal law provides clear protections for how faith-based organizations can use their property to support their mission. This is an important case for religious freedom.”

The Park Hills zoning board initially allowed the church to move forward with the plans, despite a town ordinance that restricts land use for certain spaces to arterial streets.

Neighbors who had raised concerns that the 39-foot grotto would worsen traffic problems sued, arguing that granting the conditional use permit violated state and federal law.

A state judge sided with the church, but the Kentucky Court of Appeals reversed.

Affirming that ruling, the Kentucky Supreme Court said the ordinance did not substantially infringe on the church’s rights because it could construct a smaller shrine on its existing plot. It also noted that the church was aware of the prohibition before it sought the permit.

The church argued in its petition to the U.S. Supreme Court that was a misunderstanding of the RLUIPA statute and asked the justices to clarify the scope of its protections.

“The decision below exacerbates the deep fractures on what qualifies as a ‘substantial burden’ among federal and state appellate courts — a well-recognized and longstanding conflict of authority,” lawyers representing the church wrote. “Given RLUIPA’s critical role in preserving religious liberty, this Court should grant review to clarify its application in the land-use context.”

Lawyers for the neighbors had argued the church’s petition was not the proper vehicle to take up the matter.

The case is now one of several implicating religious liberty that will be heard by the Supreme Court this term, with decisions expected by summer of next year.

articles.title: Judge bars future Reflecting Pool charges against former Olympian
articles.summary: The federal case against a former Olympian accused by the Trump administration of damaging the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool is officially dead after a Washington, D.C., judge ruled Thursday that the Department of Justice (DOJ) cannot try to charge him again in the future. Superior Court Judge Todd Edelman dismissed the case against David Hearn…
articles.body:
The federal case against a former Olympian accused by the Trump administration of damaging the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool is officially dead after a Washington, D.C., judge ruled Thursday that the Department of Justice (DOJ) cannot try to charge him again in the future.

Superior Court Judge Todd Edelman dismissed the case against David Hearn with prejudice, writing in a 26-page order that the Olympic canoeist faced a “unique possibility” that the government would attempt to revive the case in response to “political pressure” from President Trump.

“The Court respects the authority of the Office of the United States Attorney to decide which cases to prosecute and which to dismiss,” Edelman wrote. “However, in the exceptional circumstances posed by this case, the government has no right to retain the ability to compound the errors it has already made, or even to threaten to do so, at Mr. Hearn’s expense.”

Hearn was initially charged with felony destruction of property for allegedly ripping a piece of sealant from the pool, but U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro backed away from the prosecution in late July after concluding a rushed and botched installation was likely responsible for the damage.

Edelman granted that request in early August but deferred a decision on whether prosecutors should be allowed to charge him again at a later date. Hearn’s attorneys had asked that the case be closed for good.

“This decision is a victory for the rule of law and for an innocent American seeking justice,” the canoeist’s defense team said in a statement on Thursday.

Pirro’s decision drew furor from Trump, who lashed out at his longtime ally several times as he publicly urged her to reconsider.

“She folded like an umbrella,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office on Aug. 3, saying she “choked.” Trump also took aim at Hearn, referencing his prior donations to Democrats through the ActBlue fundraising platform, and he criticized one of Hearn’s attorneys, Norm Eisen.

Edelman pressed DOJ lawyers during a hearing last month to explain how the president’s comments could be construed as “anything other than pressuring your office, your boss and the three of you to charge Mr. Hearn, recharge Mr. Hearn with what you had decided to be a meritless prosecution.”

The government’s lawyers acknowledged during that hearing that prosecutors had no additional evidence against Hearn but wanted to reserve the option to pursue charges again if some arose.

Edelman rejected that possibility, saying it would have put Hearn in an “acutely vulnerable position.”

“Should the Court dismiss this case in a fashion that allows the government to reinitiate prosecution in the future, the Court would be exposing him to the risk that, due to pressure from the President of the United States apparently motivated at least in part by Mr. Hearn’s political views, he would again be charged with a crime that prosecutors have determined he did not commit,” the judge wrote.
