articles.title: Can you measure a Congress’s success?
articles.summary: While Speaker Mike Johnson defended the 118th Congress as highly productive, critics and lawmakers suggested that the institution’s focus has shifted from effective legislating to partisan social media pugilism.
articles.body:
The day after Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) dismissed the House early for its pre-election recess, Democrats lambasted him for presiding over a “do nothing Congress” with little to show for itself.

In rebuttal, the Speaker claimed the current House has been the second most productive in the history of the institution, and the most productive in the last 80 years. Those claims are open to some dispute.

Much depends on how you define legislative productivity. The Speaker claims that the House has passed over 900 pieces of legislation , 700 of which remain stuck in the Senate. Not all could become law. But as of Aug. 31, of the 732 House-passed bills and joint resolutions that could become law, only 111 had. According to a Washington Post analysis, the Democratic 115th Congress (2017 through 2018) passed the most bills into law at 580 . The Republican 118th Congress (2023 through 2024), passed the fewest at 274.

With all the crossfire of legislative numbers, one can only wonder what really determines a Congress’s success or failure. Most importantly, how do the metrics affect the state of the nation, or even influence the outcomes of individual congressional races and control of the two houses next year?

Some non-partisan groups argue that, in addition to the number of laws passed, success of Congress should also be based on the budgetary impact of key legislation, the social change it produces, and how it enables members to advance their agendas.

The easy answer to these big questions is that it is all in the eye of the beholder. Perceptions of Congress are relative and depend on your political and personal perspectives. The more complex answer is that the success or failure of a Congress is not quantifiable, no matter how many variables you factor into your equation. Ultimately, neither pre-election opinion polls nor election results will settle the question. Only history will make that final determination.

In last Sunday’s New York Times magazine , longtime Congress watcher and journalist Robert Draper published a piece, “How Congress Fell Apart,” and subtitled, “An Inside Account from Lawmakers of Both Parties About How America’s Legislative Branch Descended Into Total Dysfunction.”

Based on overwhelming negative public perceptions that Congress is not doing its intended job and interviews with 30 current and former members from both parties and key staff, Draper concludes that the big factor in the decline is the transformation of the first branch from a culture of legislating to one of social media pugilism. As Rep. Dave Joyce (R-Ohio) put it, “What you see now are too many people who come in viewing Congress as their green screen,” and “they’re going to make a name for themselves and don’t give a damn about anything else.”

Former Rep. Sean Patrick Maloney (D-N.Y.) observed that there are two business models in Congress: “One business model is legislating. … The other business model is being a social media influencer.” Rep. Julia Brownley (D-Calif.) underscored that point, “People now want scrappy fighters. … The scrappy fighter as opposed to the legislator — scrappy wins.”

Rep. Michael McCaul (R-Texas), who is retiring after 22 years, concurred. “You’re elected not to get along with the other side and get good things done for the country,” he said. “You’re elected to fight and kill the other side.”

Ironically, Draper’s piece shows a note of hope in its final pages in recounting how a bipartisan housing bill passed both chambers after much back and forth bargaining and compromises. The legislation initially had President Trump’s support, though he cooled on it toward the end to prioritize his “SAVE America Act” election changes.

Even though Trump downplayed the housing bills as “ of minor importance ,” he was finally persuaded by Johnson not to veto it. Johnson told Trump the bill gave Republicans a strong economic message to campaign on. So, after the Constitution’s requisite ten-day layover at the White House, the “The 21st Century Road to Housing Act,” became law without Trump’s signature.

Such bipartisan cooperation is rarely heard of anymore, but it is a sign that members can and do still work quietly across the aisle to get things done for the country. It may get little attention and credit from the public but will still be counted as one significant measure of success for this Congress which has little else to tout.

Don Wolfensberger is a 28-year congressional staff veteran culminating as chief of staff of the House Rules Committee. He is author of “Congress and the People: Deliberative Democracy on Trial” and “Changing Cultures in Congress: From Fair Play to Power Plays.”

articles.title: Renee Good’s family, partner sue for damages
articles.summary: The family and partner of Renee Good, the 37-year-old mother killed by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer in Minneapolis, filed lawsuits Wednesday against the federal government and President Trump for damages following the shooting. Good was fatally shot on Jan. 7 during the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) immigration crackdown in Minnesota called…
articles.body:
The family and partner of Renee Good, the 37-year-old mother killed by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer in Minneapolis, filed lawsuits Wednesday against the federal government and President Trump for damages following the shooting.

Good was fatally shot on Jan. 7 during the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) immigration crackdown in Minnesota called Operation Metro Surge .

One of the lawsuits — which named former DHS Secretary Kristi Noem, other Trump administration officials and the officers involved in the shooting — said the operation was “designed to be a violent and discriminatory campaign targeted at Minnesotans on the basis of race and national origin.”

“Renee was one of those casualties,” the lawyers for Good’s family continued.

The other lawsuit named the “United States of America” as the defendant, which allows Good’s next of kin to sue the federal government for personal injury.

This complaint cited the Hennepin County medical examiner who ruled Good’s death as a homicide following a private autopsy and the office finding “three clear gunshot wound paths” to her body.

“Each of Ross’s three shots was fired in violation” of DHS mandatory policy, which permits officers to use force only when “no reasonably effective, safe, and feasible alternative appears to exist,” the lawyers for Good’s partner, Becca Good, wrote, referencing one of the officers, Jonathan Ross.

Video from bystanders showed an officer approaching an SUV stopped across the middle of the road, demanding Good open the door before he grabbed the handle of the vehicle.

Good’s vehicle begins to pull forward and a different ICE officer standing in front of the vehicle pulls his weapon and immediately fires multiple shots into the vehicle at close range, jumping back as the vehicle moves toward him. The SUV then sped into two cars parked on a curb nearby before crashing to a stop.

The lawsuit alleged Ross, the officer who shot and killed Good, also shouted obscenities at the woman while she pulled forward, yelling “f‑‑‑ing b‑‑‑‑.”

Video appeared to show Good’s neighbor, a doctor, being told to step back after he offered medical care for her twice.

Her death, and another shooting involving the killing of 37-year-old Alex Pretti by an ICE officer in Minneapolis a week later, sparked waves of intense protests across the state.

ICE and DHS did not respond immediately to The Hill’s request for comment.

articles.title: A new Medicare program opened the door to obesity treatment — keep it open
articles.summary: More than 600,000 Medicare beneficiaries have enrolled in the Medicare GLP-1 Bridge program since its launch on July 1, 2026, providing eligible seniors with expanded access to obesity medications.
articles.body:
For too many people affected by obesity, the biggest barrier to treatment isn’t whether effective options exist. It’s whether they can access them.

For older adults, that barrier has been especially difficult to overcome.

Obesity treatment has advanced dramatically in recent years, but Medicare coverage has not kept pace. That began to change July 1, 2026, with the launch of the Medicare GLP-1 Bridge program , giving eligible beneficiaries access to obesity medications that, for many, had previously been out of reach because of cost or lack of coverage.

The response tells us something important.

In just two months, more than 600,000 Medicare beneficiaries have enrolled . Initial data indicate that most had never had access to GLP-1 medications for obesity. That is not simply strong enrollment. It is evidence of a need that has gone unmet for far too long.

Through the Bridge Program, eligible Medicare Part D beneficiaries can access certain GLP-1 medications for obesity with a $50 monthly co-pay . The program runs through the end of next year.

Our organization welcomes this progress. It is a bridge. But where will that bridge take us?

Obesity is a complex, chronic disease affecting 40 percent of Americans . Like people living with any other chronic disease, people affected by obesity need access to comprehensive, evidence-based care. Yet outdated policies and persistent stigma have stood between people and treatments that could improve their health and quality of life.

GLP-1 medications are one treatment option. They are not appropriate for everyone, nor are they the only way to treat obesity. The right treatment is a decision that should be made by individuals and their healthcare providers. Insurance coverage should not make that decision for them.

That is why the Bridge Program matters. But what happens next matters even more. The program is temporary. Over the next 15 months, we have an opportunity to demonstrate what happens when people affected by obesity have greater access to evidence-based treatment. We also have a responsibility to ensure that when this bridge ends, people are not sent backward.

Those affected by obesity deserve the same opportunity to access appropriate treatment as people living with other chronic diseases. They deserve to make healthcare decisions with their providers based on science and their individual needs — not stigma, cost or outdated coverage restrictions.

The Medicare GLP-1 Bridge Program is meaningful progress. Now we need to build on it. Every bridge is supposed to take us somewhere. This one should lead to comprehensive, affordable and lasting access to obesity care. We must make sure it does.

Joseph Nadglowski is the president and CEO of the Obesity Action Coalition .

articles.title: Capitol Hill is a ghost town until November
articles.summary: Plus: 💉The failed execution of Christa Pike {beacon} It’s Thursday, and National Pumpkin Spice Day. This is maybe the fifth time we’ve written about pumpkin spice, but we thought you should know. In today’s issue: Senate goes on midterm recess Trump’s Supreme Court regrets FCC OKs taxpayer-funded ads Christa Pike’s execution snafu Programming…
articles.body:
It’s Thursday, and National Pumpkin Spice Day. This is maybe the fifth time we’ve written about pumpkin spice, but we thought you should know.

Programming note : We’re Claire Leibowitz and Abigail Walker, filling in for Cate today. Please send your tips, comments and story ideas to cleibowitz@thehill.com or awalker@thehill.com .

The Senate adjourned Wednesday night until the week of Nov. 9, after the midterm elections. Vulnerable Republicans are returning home to campaign as fears over losing their majority arise, The Hill’s Alexander Bolton reports .

Senators adjourned after confirming President Trump’s Labor secretary pick, Keith Sonderling.

What’s left for the lame – duck session ?: The annual defense authorization bill, the extension of expired surveillance authorities under the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act and other high-profile items have been left behind.

There are also 12 appropriations bills at stake, and the government’s funding plan ends on Dec. 11.

Senators speak up: Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) said the adjournment “breaks my heart.”

“It’s bad planning. We should have started after we passed One Big Beautiful Bill [in July 2025], planning what we wanted to do and how we were going to get it done,” he added.

But vulnerable GOP senators, including Dan Sullivan (Alaska), Roger Marshall (Kan.), Pete Ricketts (Neb.) and Susan Collins (Maine) are excited to return to the campaign trail.

“I think everybody’s nervous about their races,” Kennedy said. “It’s a weird year. I don’t know how these things are going to turn out.”

“I’ve done polling in my own state, and it’s a pretty red state, but people all across the political spectrum are very unsettled,” he added.

Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) predicted that Senate Republican losses will be “manageable” if “we let candidates execute down the stretch,” and that being in Washington can hurt their races.

“Every time you’re here, it’s a fundraiser you can’t host or it’s a town hall you can’t speak at. We need to get them back in the state. Invariably, the people who want to stick here, they all have one thing in common: They’re not up [for reelection] this cycle,” he said.

Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) said the lame-duck session will be a “golden era” for Republicans.

When the Senate returns, they will have only eight legislative days in November and 14 days in December to square away its agenda. And that includes Fridays, which aren’t typically workdays.

Trump on Thursday said he regrets nominating Justices Neil Gorsuch , Amy Coney Barrett and Brett Kavanaugh to the Supreme Court.

“They voted against me too often,” the president told Time magazine . “I gave them the position of a lifetime, and they vote against me often. They vote for me too.”

He also commented that the Democratic justices “stick like glue” when they vote.

Sore spots: Trump criticized the high court for striking down his tariffs in February in a 6-3 decision.

Justices also ruled against his birthright citizenship order in June in a 6-3 decision.

And most recently, the court blocked his mail-in voting overhaul that focused on the U.S. Postal Service’s inability to implement his desired changes ahead of November’s elections.

“These are not the people I interviewed to serve on the United States Supreme Court, they are merely a shell of their original selves,” Trump wrote a couple of weeks ago on Truth Social.

Quite the Time (interview) : The president also discussed that he has not ruled out invoking the Insurrection Act or declaring a national emergency ahead of midterms.

“I’m not committing to anything,” Trump said in the interview when asked about the limits of his presidential power. “We’re going to see how it plays out in court.”

This isn’t his first time at the rodeo. He threatened to deploy troops to Minneapolis after an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer shot and killed U.S. citizen Renee Good in January.

In June 2025, he said he would “certainly” invoke the act in response to anti-ICE demonstrations in the streets of Los Angeles, and again about similar protests in Portland, Ore., in October.

Trump also considered sending troops to Minneapolis after George Floyd was killed by police in 2020.

Federal Communications Commission (FCC) leader Brendan Carr dismissed concerns about new taxpayer-funded Trump ads.

“There’s nothing in there that strikes me as out of the ordinary or that would merit any sort of FCC review,” Carr said. “There are groups on the left that have long worked and pushed to weaponize the FCC’s license renewal process.”

The head of the FCC also described the ads as “normal PSAs that don’t raise any red flags.”

The political ads, which first aired Sunday during two NFL games, feature the president condemning “communism, socialism and Marxism in America.”

Sens. Patty Murray (D-Wash.) and Chris Murphy (D-Conn.) on Tuesday demanded that the ads be removed and requested a precise breakdown of how taxpayer money was used to fund them.

“These ads need to immediately come off the air, taxpayers need to be paid back for this theft, and everyone responsible needs to be held accountable for this corrupt and illegal propaganda,” the pair wrote in their letter to Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Markwayne Mullin .

Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee (R) paused the use of capital punishment in the state following the failed execution of convicted murderer Christa Pike.

“Carrying out a lawfully imposed sentence is among the State’s most serious responsibilities, and the people of Tennessee expect it to be done in a manner that is not only legal and constitutional, but is effective,” the governor said in a statement, according to The Associated Press.

The outlet reported that Pike was still alive after receiving two doses of the lethal injection, pentobarbital, on Wednesday.

Her lawyers said the attempted execution caused “unnecessary agony” and violated Pike’s constitutional “right to be executed free of cruel and unusual punishment.”

Lee added that Tennessee would conduct a “comprehensive, third-party review to determine exactly what occurred” and halt all remaining executions set to be carried out this year.

A new survey found that 73 percent of Americans disapprove of Trump’s handling of the economy. The data, released by The Associated Press/NORC Research Center, also found that 65 percent of respondents blame the president’s policies for higher prices.

The Supreme Court on Thursday announced it will decide the legality of Trump’s mandatory detention policy , which argues that anyone in the country unlawfully can be detained without bond, even if they’ve been in the U.S. for years.

New polling revealed a record low number of Americans see a college education as important. The Gallup poll, published Thursday, found that 31 percent of respondents see a college degree as “very important,” 4 points lower than in 2025.

The Associated Press : German firm claims world record for tallest wind turbine

NBC News : Ex-fraternity leader at an Arizona university gets jail time after pledge died of alcohol poisoning

The New York Times : A.I. Anxiety Is Showing Up in Therapy

Politico : A new Bolsonaro could pull Brazil away from Europe — and toward Trump

The House and Senate are out. President Trump is in Texas, Oklahoma and Washington. (All times EDT)

articles.title: Jackson holds edge over Collins in Maine Senate race: Poll
articles.summary: Maine Democratic Senate candidate Troy Jackson is narrowly leading Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) in the race for her seat, according to a new survey. In the AARP poll, 50 percent of respondents said they were “definitely,” “probably” or leaning toward casting their ballot for Jackson if the election occurred that day, and 47 percent said…
articles.body:
Maine Democratic Senate candidate Troy Jackson is narrowly leading Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) in the race for her seat, according to a new survey.

In the AARP poll, 50 percent of respondents said they were “definitely,” “probably” or leaning toward casting their ballot for Jackson if the election occurred that day, and 47 percent said the same of Collins. One percent said they would choose a different candidate, and 3 percent were not sure or undecided.

The poll had a margin of error of 3.13 percentage points.

The AARP poll comes amid rocky political territory for Republicans with the midterms about a month out. Challenges facing the GOP include President Trump’s sliding approval rating, the unpopular war in Iran, which has lasted for more than half the year, and concerns about the economy.

Jackson, a former Maine state Senate president, formally clinched the Democratic nomination in July to challenge Collins in the general election. Democrats in Maine mostly came together around Jackson before a convention to replace former candidate Graham Platner, whose campaign was weighed down by multiple scandals.

The Senate race in Maine is considered a “toss up” by the nonpartisan election handicapper Cook Political Report, and former Vice President Kamala Harris won the state in the 2024 presidential election.

The AARP poll also found Democratic candidate Hannah Pingree leading in the governor’s race in Maine. Fifty-two percent of respondents supported her, while 39 percent backed her Republican opponent, Robert Charles, and 6 percent backed Independent Rick Bennett.

The AARP poll took place from Sept. 20-22 and featured 982 likely voters in Maine.

articles.title: The flying public needs a 21st century aviation system
articles.summary: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has requested $30 billion from Congress to complete essential upgrades to the nation’s aging air traffic control infrastructure following recent travel disruptions in the Northeast.
articles.body:
Flyers across the Northeast recently witnessed firsthand why America’s aviation system is in desperate need of an upgrade. A telecommunications failure, compounded by existing problems with a backup connection, left thousands of passengers from Philadelphia to Boston stranded on the tarmac.

Pointing to the decades-old technology running our airspace, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy offered a blunt assessment : “this is not shocking.” But he added that with the right funding from Congress, Uncle Sam can “prevent disruptions like this in the future.”

Although the Trump administration is working to shore up many of these vulnerabilities across the National Airspace System, completing the job will require continued funding from Congress.

Just over a year ago, the Federal Aviation Administration kickstarted an effort to build an “Envy of the World” air traffic control network to the tune of $12.5 billion. The goal is to replace decades-old infrastructure with technology capable of handling today’s passenger volumes with a fraction of the disruptions.

To date, roughly two-thirds of aging copper wires have been replaced by fiber optic cables or wireless technology, helping pilots communicate more effectively with controllers on the ground. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford expects this portion of the modernization project to be completed by this time next year.

Meanwhile, dozens of new surface-awareness systems have been installed, giving personnel a clearer picture of aircraft and vehicles moving across runways and taxiways. These cutting-edge tools provide efficiency — but they are only half of the equation.

Additional funds are needed to begin the next phase of the modernization overhaul. This includes a modern air traffic flow management system and AI-powered software to better predict when disruptions on the tarmac could occur. The tech is currently being debuted at airports in the D.C.-area with hopes that it can be extended to hubs nationwide.

How much is needed to finish these and other infrastructure upgrades? Duffy recently requested $30 billion in funding.

The additional investment is sorely needed. The FAA has warned that it is “already starting to delay phase two and ⁠phase three because of lack of funding.” Now more than ever, Congress needs to step up and provide a second down-payment on modernization to avoid further delays.

Several lawmakers have already signaled their willingness to support it. During a recent House Appropriations Committee hearing, Transportation-HUD subcommittee chairman Steve Womack (R-Ark.) told the FAA chief “we are here to be a partner in the effort.”

House Appropriations Chairman Tom Cole (R-Okla.) similarly emphasized Congress’s role in providing necessary investment and oversight, ensuring the FAA has the “resources, workforce, and capabilities” needed to carry out its mission.

While Republicans broadly back the current effort, modernization has no shortage of support from the other side. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) has previously called attention to our outdated skies, while former President Joe Biden proposed his own plan to modernize America’s air traffic control network.

The upcoming December budget negotiations could give appropriators an opportunity to begin satisfying the FAA’s request. Congress could also consider passing a standalone funding package. Regardless of which path lawmakers take, continuing to keep modernization efforts moving will prove to be a good return on taxpayer investment.

Compared to fixing old equipment or patching outdated software, the money would translate to tangible benefits for the flying public. Sick of air traffic control delays or communications failures that can add hours to a trip and fumble connections? This is the answer.

The latest aviation disruptions across the Northeast serve as another reminder that relying on older air traffic control infrastructure can cause real headaches for travelers. The Department of Transportation is already working to overhaul it. Now, funding from Congress must keep pace.

Jackson Shedelbower is the executive director of the Center for Transportation Policy.

articles.title: Judge rules officers have no standing to sue over Capitol Jan. 6 plaque
articles.summary: A federal judge ruled Wednesday that two police officers who defended the U.S. Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021, have no standing to sue over their names — and those of other first responders — not appearing on a plaque commemorating law enforcement’s response to the attack. U.S. District Judge Dabney Friedrich said she would grant…
articles.body:
A federal judge ruled Wednesday that two police officers who defended the U.S. Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021, have no standing to sue over their names — and those of other first responders — not appearing on a plaque commemorating law enforcement’s response to the attack.

U.S. District Judge Dabney Friedrich said she would grant the Architect of the Capitol’s motion to dismiss the pair’s lawsuit “for lack of jurisdiction.”

The two officers, former U.S. Capitol Police officer Harry Dunn and active District of Columbia Metropolitan Police officer Daniel Hodges, sued the architect over the missing names, as the plaque only lists law enforcement agencies and organizations that sent personnel to defend the Capitol “alongside a QR code that visitors may scan to access the officers’ names,” court documents show.

Text on the plaque reads: “On behalf of a grateful Congress, this plaque honors the extraordinary individuals who bravely protected and defended this symbol of democracy on January 6, 2021. Their heroism will never be forgotten.”

The plaque was also planned to be permanently visible “on the western front of the Capitol” but has been temporarily displayed in “the non-public Senate wing” as of March.

Friedrich, an appointee of former President George W. Bush, noted that standing is “assessed from the time of the complaint.”

“Because the officers lacked standing when they commenced this action, this court lacks subject-matter jurisdiction and must dismiss the case,” she wrote.

She asserted that neither officer had a cognizable injury at the time of the plaque’s installation and dismissed their argument that the architect had “exacerbated ‘psychic injuries'” they have experienced since Jan. 6. Dunn and Hodges also argued that not recognizing individual service emboldened others to “harass them and disparage” the officers’ response.

“To be sure, the officers have a far more personal connection to the plaque than the public at large,” Friedrich wrote. “They are not ‘just any person’ … they are among the very officers Congress sought to honor. That gives them an understandable and deeply personal interest in whether the government recognizes their service in the manner Congress prescribed.”

“But Article II standing ‘is not measured by the intensity of the litigant’s interest, ‘ ” she continued. “It requires an injury in fact … Even if the Architect’s failure to install the plaque contributed to the officers’ injuries, the officers would need to show that mandating its installation would be ‘likely’ to alleviate those injuries.”

The officers initially filed a lawsuit over a delay in installing the plaque. Former President Biden signed a law in 2022 requesting a plaque to honor the officers who defended the Capitol during the attack, giving its installation a one-year deadline. But the plaque was never erected.

It was finally installed in March of this year, with the years-long delay prompting Hodges and Dunn to separately sue the Architect of the Capitol to “prominently display” the memorial in a “publicly accessible” area in the Senate wing. The officers argued that the plaque was “ hidden .”

articles.title: Trump says he rejected Secret Service plan to tear down Oval Office
articles.summary: President Trump said he told the Secret Service that he wouldn’t allow for the Oval Office to be demolished. articles.body:
President Trump said he told the Secret Service that he wouldn’t allow for the Oval Office to be demolished.

Trump was asked what he would miss the most about the White House when he leaves office at the end of his second term, and the president spoke about the historic West Wing office.

“This beautiful room that nobody should be allowed to rip down,” he said. “The Oval Office.”

Trump said he had seen Secret Service agents looking around the room.

“And I say, ‘What are you guys looking at?’ ‘Sir, we think the Oval Office should be taken down, and we’ll build a new one, sir,'” he told Time magazine in an interview published Thursday .

“I said, ‘My a–, you can’t build a new one. This is a special place,'” the president continued.

Trump decked out the Oval Office with gold appliques and gold frames, along with gold trim to the crown molding. He decked out the presidential seal on the Oval Office’s ceiling with gold and put gold signage outside the door saying, “The Oval Office.”

He said in the interview that he’s been considering landmark status for the Oval Office.

“I’ve been asking Susie for six months to give me a statement. Will we save this room? Will we make it a federal landmark?” Trump said, referring to his chief of staff, Susie Wiles.

While he feels strongly about the Oval Office, he has made other changes to the White House.

Last October he demolished the East Wing to make space for a 90,000-square-foot ballroom. He also paved over the Rose Garden, adding tables and chairs, and redid the Palm Room.

He added gold-framed photos of past presidents along the West Wing Walkway and Colonnade, and replaced its flooring with dark granite.

The president also made changes to the Cabinet room and added flags to the North and South lawns, along with a helipad .

In his interview he said the White House was a “dump” that he fixed up.

“The White House is a very special symbol,” he said. “It’s a symbol of America. It’s a symbol of our greatness.”

“And I said, ‘I got to fix it.’ And I do that better than anybody else,” Trump added. “Maybe I do it better than anything I do, and it’s easy for me. It’s actually relaxing. You know, for a lot of people, it drives them crazy.”

articles.body:
Well, one Democratic Senate candidate is running away from the platform of the Democratic Socialists of America, even though she is a member of the group. That’s Florida’s Angie Nixon, who had this to say to Bloomberg. Watch .

I actually think that’s quite revealing of the DSA’s agenda: They do want to abolish prison for actual criminals, but they need to retain prisons so they can jail their opponents. In that way, the democratic socialists are proving that they’re just normal socialists.

It’s perfectly proper for the state to investigate that, but a grand jury declined to indict Moody and said she wasn’t responsible for it. Socialists don’t care about the normal and standard operations of the justice system, however, since they want to abolish our entire Constitution and just do whatever they want.

And don’t let Angie Nixon fool you, that is exactly what she will try to do if the left continues to take over the Democratic Party. Theirs is a deeply radical agenda, and a dangerous one. More Americans need to take notice, because things are getting a bit dire. If recent polls are to be believed, Democrats are headed for huge gains in the midterms . Now places like Ohio and Iowa seem up for grabs. If the Democratic Party wins big, the left will be emboldened to go further and further. The DSA’s agenda is only the beginning.

articles.title: Ken Paxton reveals GOP polling ‘dropped’ after midterm convention: NYT
articles.summary: So, just to recap: Trump brings Republicans to Texas for a convention designed to help Republican candidates, like Ken Paxton. Then Paxton privately says his poll numbers dropped after said convention. And at the convention, the president is essentially doing a roast of his own Senate candidate’s wardrobe, speaking style and appearance before ultimately telling voters they should still elect him.
articles.body:
If you want to know how Republicans are feeling about the president’s impact on the midterm elections, The New York Times is letting us know.

Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton was caught on leaked audio talking about President Trump’s midterm convention in Dallas and, according to Paxton himself, it did not exactly move the needle in the direction Republicans wanted. The Times reports that the audio said:

“So to be honest with you, the numbers — when we did that convention — it dropped our numbers.”

“Everybody’s numbers dropped. Right now, yeah, not good.”

Let’s not forget Paxton’s entire campaign is built around an endorsement from the president, but I guess now that he realizes what the rest of America realizes: that the policies aren’t working. Now he wants to avoid being tied to Trump.

It gets even more awkward when you remember what happened at that very convention Paxton is referring to. The president actually made fun of him while showing support:

“The fact is that some may not like the way he dresses. I don’t,” said Trump. “They may not like the way he talks.”

So, just to recap: Trump brings Republicans to Texas for a convention designed to help Republican candidates, like Ken Paxton. Then Paxton privately says his poll numbers dropped after said convention. And at the convention, the president is essentially doing a roast of his own Senate candidate’s wardrobe, speaking style and appearance before ultimately telling voters they should still elect him.

Vice President Vance campaigned in South Texas just yesterday, an area where Trump won overwhelmingly in 2024. Perhaps the president’s poor decisions are the exact reason that the VP is spending valuable campaign time shoring up a state that Republicans have long considered safely red.

It’s clear that the Trump brand is not helping Republican candidates in places where voters are being asked to make a choice about their local representative, not the president. The Wall Street Journal’s latest poll puts Trump’s approval at just 37 percent, the lowest pre-midterm approval rating for any president in the Journal’s poll going back to 1990 .

And a recent NBC News poll found 43 percent of registered voters said their midterm vote would be a signal of opposition to Trump — the highest level recorded in that question since NBC began asking it in 1998.

Now let’s look at all the money spent. More than $155 million has been spent or reserved for television and digital advertising supporting Paxton, according to AdImpact, and it hasn’t been effective in giving him a strong lead against James Talarico. That is a lot of money to spend trying to convince Texas voters that everything is fine.

I mean, Republicans can spend millions. They can bring in the vice president. Trump can hold a convention and tell voters to support his candidates, but none of that changes what voters are experiencing: a bad economy, high gas prices, higher medical insurance premiums…

Paxton’s leaked comments don’t prove every Republican candidate believes Trump is hurting them, of course, but the fact that he is saying this is certainly revealing.

I’m going to say it again: maybe it’s policies that actually make people feel better about their lives, not the rallies, not the promise of $5,000 checks, not the millions political action committees spend. The Republican Party is not doing a great job laying out how the policies pushed by this administration are positively affecting anyone.

And, in Paxton’s case, perhaps a campaign that comes with a little less political baggage wouldn’t hurt either.

Lindsey Granger is a NewsNation contributor and co-host of The Hill’s commentary show “Rising.” This column is an edited transcription of her on-air commentary.

articles.body:
Wisconsin Democratic gubernatorial candidate David Crowley is nearly tied with his Republican opponent, Rep. Tom Tiffany (Wis.), according to a new poll.

In the Marquette University Law School Wisconsin poll , 46 percent of respondents said they would cast their ballots for Crowley if the election occurred that day, while 45 percent said the same of Tiffany. Nine percent were undecided.

The margin of error in the poll is plus or minus 4.3 percentage points.

Wisconsin, which currently has a Democratic governor, was won by President Trump in the last presidential election . The state has developed a swing state reputation in the last decade.

However, Republicans are facing a challenging electoral environment this year as they head into the midterms. The GOP is dealing with issues like Trump’s slipping approval rating, the unpopular war in Iran that just passed the seven-month mark and economic concerns.

Last week, Tiffany reiterated his calls to Trump to end the fighting in Iran. FOX6 News Milwaukee reporter Jason Calvi pressed the Wisconsin Republican about why he had not supported a war powers resolution on multiple occasions in the House, despite pushing for an end to the conflict.

“The president has final say in regards to this,” Tiffany replied, according to a video shared by Calvi on social media.

“I just believe that we should be exiting Iran, that it’s time to move on,” the GOP lawmaker added. “We’ve degraded their nuclear facilities. We degraded their military. Most of their ships are at the bottom of the ocean. Time to come home, take care of business here in America.”

The Marquette Law poll took place from Sept. 16-23 and featured 843 registered voters in Wisconsin.

articles.body:
Former Rep. Mary Peltola (D-Alaska) launched a new campaign ad that notably distances herself from the Democratic Party, telling voters to “forget party, forget politics.”

“With me, Alaska comes first,” Peltola said in the ad , before touting her “A rating” from the National Rifle Association (NRA). “I took on Joe Biden to secure the border and push through Alaska’s largest oil project in decades.”

“It’s why I’ve got no tolerance for any politician who uses their office to get rich,” she concluded.

Peltola is an unlikely challenger against incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska). Her moderate, Alaska-first bid has drawn widespread support in the Last Frontier, fueling Democrats’ hopes of flipping the seat.

Alaska has sided with President Trump in each of his three presidential races. In 2024, Peltola lost Alaska’s at-large House seat to Republican Rep. Nick Begich. The state has also elected a Democrat to the Senate just once in the past 50 years.

Cook Political Report rates this year’s race as a “toss-up,” writing in its race summary that Peltola is “well-positioned.”

An AARP poll conducted by pollsters Fabrizio Ward and Impact Research found Peltola ahead of Sullivan at 46 percent support to his 41 percent, with 7 percent of respondents undecided.

She found major ground when she focused her campaign around opposition to large-scale trawling, which has been credited as a major reason for stocks of salmon, crab and halibut running low in critical regions of the state.

In September, Peltola’s campaign faced controversy for a New York Times report that detailed profane outbursts and displays of anger throughout the campaign and her former congressional office, citing several former Peltola aides who requested anonymity.

Her campaign denied the allegations concerning the workplace environment but did acknowledge that she “sometimes struggled to deal with her grief” after the 2023 deaths of her mother and husband . The campaign also told the Times that Peltola had used an ableist slur and regretted doing so, but it denied allegations that she had used a homophobic slur.

articles.title: Trump slams Time staff during interview for not asking ‘one f‑‑‑ing positive question’
articles.summary: President Trump slammed Time’s staff during a lengthy interview published Thursday, where he ripped into them for not asking him “one f‑‑‑ing positive question.” He was asked about Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) returning to the Senate after months away while recuperating from a fall he suffered at home in June, and whether the lawmaker should…
articles.body:
President Trump slammed Time’s staff during a lengthy interview published Thursday, where he ripped into them for not asking him “one f‑‑‑ing positive question.”

He was asked about Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) returning to the Senate after months away while recuperating from a fall he suffered at home in June, and whether the lawmaker should resign due to his condition. But the president appeared to still be answering a previous question about pardoning members of his Cabinet if Democrats retake Congress in November.

“It was a disappointment to a lot of Republicans. So that’s just –– well, Sleepy Joe gave pardons to everybody. He gave them to Fauci,” Trump said, referring to former President Biden and former White House medical adviser Dr. Anthony Fauci. “He gave them to this.”

“But you mean I’m not allowed to give them, but Sleepy Joe’s allowed to give them?” Trump asked. “This ain’t gonna be much of a story. Here we are doing this. You haven’t asked me one f‑‑‑ing positive question. All of this. What about this? What about that? What about that? What about this? All negative.”

He shifted to reacting to previous questions about the condition of the White House, saying that it leaked when it rained and people were “walking under –– crap was falling off it all the time.”

“Now it’s perfect, and I would say that I should be given credit for fixing the White House because I’m also doing very well with the war,” he said. “I’m doing very well with another war that we already won, Venezuela. Do you notice you haven’t asked me a question about Venezuela?”

Reporters pushed back, saying he asked about the Latin American country earlier in the interview. Trump was asked about his meeting with Venezuelan interim President Delcy Rodríguez at the United Nations General Assembly and whether they talked about holding elections in her country, though he mentioned the country earlier in the discussion.

“No, but I’m just thinking to myself, ‘fake news.’ But I have a lot of respect. I like the owner, good guy. But I don’t understand. I’m sitting here. I’ve done all this stuff,” Trump said, before adding that he made the White House “beautiful again.”

The interview touched on a wide array of issues, from the midterm elections to his immigration agenda. He told the staffers he has not ruled out demolishing the Kennedy Center as he fights to keep his name on the building in court, and he refused to rule out invoking the Insurrection Act around the midterms.

The president has lashed out at the press before, but the remarks come amid his ongoing tensions with CNN by barring its reporters from joining the White House press pool. The latest successful attempt to do so on Thursday comes after a federal judge lifted a ban Trump implemented on the outlet, Politico and MS NOW from covering his administration.

Trump banned all three outlets two weeks ago from working from the White House over what he called their publishing of “fake news.” He and Attorney General Todd Blanche have argued it could amount to a national security issue regarding U.S. relations with other nations. Blanche suggested that reporting on the president “doesn’t have to be good” or all positive, but Trump blasted the outlets for “negative” coverage.

“Fake News people and publications that only write negatively, and who violate our National Security by writing false and defamatory stories with unknown ‘sources,’ shouldn’t be allowed access to the most important Office anywhere in the World,” Trump wrote on Truth Social the day he banned the outlets.

The move ignited backlash from lawmakers, news outlets like Fox News and free speech advocates. Former White House Correspondents’ Association president Weijia Jiang told Fox News that an attack on the three outlets was “ an attack on everyone. “

articles.body:
President Trump threatened Thursday that Iran will cease to exist if its leaders do not sign a peace deal with the U.S.

“Now I have to make a decision. They’ll either sign a very fair deal, or they won’t exist any longer,” Trump told reporters on the South Lawn en route to Oklahoma.

The president also told reporters that Iran could have been connected to a copilot’s alleged attempt to crash an Israel-bound airplane traveling from Dubai earlier this week.

“I would say the answer based on what I’m hearing is yes, but we’re working on it right now,” the president said.

Trump said Wednesday that he spoke “at length” with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu about the incident.

The president’s comments come after he told Time Magazine that he rejected Iran’s latest peace offer.

“It’s just not good enough, nearly,” Trump told the publication, saying he rejected the proposal in part because it only opened “some aspects” of the Strait of Hormuz.

Trump also told Time Magazine that he would not accept any proposals from Tehran that he would not have approved a year ago and said it was possible he could resume the bombing of Iran following November’s midterm elections.

articles.body:
President Trump will kick off his red-state campaign swing on Thursday afternoon with a visit to a manufacturing plant in Denton, Texas.

Trump is likely to use the stop to highlight his trade and tariff agenda, as well as the Trump administration’s efforts to boost domestic production. The visit comes as the president faces persistent concerns over the economy, with recent polls showing that his approval on the issue remains underwater .

The stop in the Lone Star State also puts Trump in the middle of a competitive Senate race between Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R), whom he backed, and Democratic state Rep. James Talarico. Paxton is expected to appear with Trump in Denton — days after he suggested in private that the GOP midterm convention last month hurt him politically.

Later Thursday, Trump will travel to Oklahoma and give remarks.

The event at Peterbilt Motors is scheduled to begin at 4 p.m. EDT.

articles.title: Hume: Republicans ‘don’t have much going for them’ ahead of midterms
articles.summary: Fox News’s Brit Hume on Wednesday said that Republicans lack momentum only a few weeks out from the midterms, with the GOP dealing with multiple political challenges as Election Day nears. “I would say that the Republicans don’t have much going for them this cycle. The polls all suggest that, the mood of the country…
articles.body:
Fox News’s Brit Hume on Wednesday said that Republicans lack momentum only a few weeks out from the midterms, with the GOP dealing with multiple political challenges as Election Day nears.

“I would say that the Republicans don’t have much going for them this cycle. The polls all suggest that, the mood of the country suggests that,” Hume told Fox News’s Bret Baier on “Special Report.”

“They do have more money than the Democrats do, which could be spent wisely, one would imagine, to help them, but this 69 percent number that you show there on cost of living, I don’t think much is going to change on cost of living over the next month,” he added, referencing poll results from Fox News that had just been shown about voters’ reasoning behind their vote in the key Michigan Senate race this year.

Hume continued, saying that cost of living circumstances “could change a little” and that “things have turned around a bit in the in the Strait of Hormuz,” referencing the key waterway for the oil industry that has been closed amid the war in Iran.

“Republicans have to worry that opinions have solidified and not in their favor, and that number suggests that that may be the case,” Hume said.

Republicans are staring down a challenging electoral environment these midterms, with President Trump’s slipping approval rating, the war in Iran stretching past the seven-month mark, polls showing they are behind in multiple races and concerns about the economy.

The conflict in Iran has driven up energy costs in the U.S., with the price of a regular gallon of gas sitting at about $4.41 on Thursday afternoon, up from about $3.16 last year at the same time, according to AAA .
